name: Baroreflex Failure

criteria.description: Volatile blood pressure with episodic severe hypertension alternating with hypotension
Volatile heart rate with episodic tachycardia
Identifiable cause of baroreflex arc damage (neck surgery, radiation, bilateral carotid body tumor resection, brainstem lesion)
Absent or markedly reduced heart rate response to blood pressure changes (absent baroreflex sensitivity)
Exaggerated pressor response to mental or physical stress

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Volatile blood pressure with absent baroreflex sensitivity, often with an identifiable cause of baroreflex arc disruption
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Must distinguish from pheochromocytoma and panic disorder. Confirmed by pharmacological baroreflex testing showing absent heart rate response to phenylephrine and nitroprusside.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Extreme blood pressure volatility with surges of severe hypertension (often >200/100 mmHg)
pathognomonic.notes: Hypertensive surges can be triggered by stress, pain, or exertion

occasional.symptomName: Hypotension during sleep or quiescent periods
occasional.notes: BP may drop to very low levels when not stressed

laboratory: Plasma catecholamines may be elevated during surges
24-hour urine catecholamines and metanephrines normal or mildly elevated (to exclude pheochromocytoma)
imaging: MRI of brainstem may show lesion in nucleus tractus solitarius (if central cause)
CT/MRI neck may show post-surgical or radiation changes
genetic: No established genetic cause in acquired cases
other: Pharmacological baroreflex testing: absent HR response to phenylephrine-induced BP rise
Pharmacological baroreflex testing: absent HR response to nitroprusside-induced BP fall
24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring: extreme BP variability
Valsalva maneuver: absent heart rate changes during phases

distinguishingFeatures: Pheochromocytoma shows adrenal mass on imaging
Baroreflex failure has absent baroreflex sensitivity on testing
Panic disorder has normal baroreflex sensitivity
BP surges in baroreflex failure are more extreme and reproducible
Essential hypertension is sustained, not episodic with extreme volatility
Baroreflex failure alternates between severe hypertension and hypotension

redFlags: Hypertensive crises reaching >250/130 mmHg (end-organ damage risk)
Concurrent bradycardia during hypertensive surge (suggests complete baroreflex failure)
History of neck radiation or bilateral carotid body surgery
New-onset extreme BP volatility after brainstem stroke
references: Biaggioni I, et al. Baroreflex failure. In: Robertson D, Biaggioni I, eds. Primer on the Autonomic Nervous System. 3rd ed. Academic Press; 2012:349-353.
Ketch T, et al. Baroreflex failure: clinical presentation and management. Curr Hypertens Rep. 2002;4(3):209-215.
Robertson D, et al. Afferent baroreflex failure in the human. J Clin Invest. 1993;91(4):1400-1413.
